strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful capability—incremental, variable-length (1 to N frame) feedforward 3D avatar reconstruction—that addresses a real limitation of prior fixed-length feedforward methods (LAM: 1 frame, Avat3r: 4 frames).

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (NeRSemble, Ava256, INSTA) and against many baselines (LAM, MonoGaussianAvatar, GaussianAvatars, Avat3r, Arc2Avatar, HeadGap, SynShot, GPAvatar), covering monocular and multi-view settings.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of sliced fusion loss, landmark tracking loss, global attention, GS fusion, and Gaussian pruning, with both quantitative tables and qualitative visualizations.

Demonstrates favorable speed-quality tradeoffs (sub-second to ~26s modeling time depending on frame count) while achieving competitive or superior PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/identity metrics relative to baselines.

Additional robustness analysis (landmark noise injection), wide-viewpoint generalization tests, and a streaming/FramePack-inspired extension for long sequences show reasonably thorough exploration of the method's behavior.
Honest discussion of limitations (FLAME topology constraints, eye gaze, wrinkles, tongue) and an ethics statement addressing potential misuse.
weaknesses: The core architecture is a fairly direct adaptation of VGGT (replacing DPT with an MLP head, adding FLAME-based positional prompts) combined with LAM-initialized attention blocks, making the technical novelty somewhat incremental/combinatorial rather than fundamentally new.

Comparison with Avat3r is not run directly (no public implementation), relying instead on numbers copied from the Avat3r paper, which raises fairness/consistency concerns (different data splits, preprocessing, hardware).

The LAM* baseline modification (altering the renderer to fuse multi-frame information) is done by the authors themselves; it's unclear whether this is an optimal-faith reimplementation of an alternative multi-frame LAM, potentially disadvantaging this baseline.

Training relies solely on the NeRSemble dataset (521 clips, 12 cameras), which may limit diversity in ethnicity, lighting, and capture conditions; generalization to truly in-the-wild data is only lightly demonstrated (a few qualitative examples).
No user studies or perceptual evaluations are included despite avatar quality being inherently subjective in some respects.
Substantial training cost (8×H100 GPUs for 14 days) is not contextualized against baseline training costs, and code/model release is promised but not verifiable at review time.
Streaming/sliding-window incremental reconstruction is only qualitatively demonstrated (Figure 11) without quantitative metrics, weakening claims about its practicality.

The paper's writing contains some redundant or imprecise phrasing and notational inconsistencies (e.g., undefined variables in equations, inconsistent use of hat notation), suggesting the manuscript could benefit from another editing pass.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical limitation of existing feedforward avatar methods: LAM is fixed to single-frame input and Avat3r is fixed to exactly 4 frames, while FastAvatar can flexibly ingest 1 to 16+ frames (monocular or multi-view) within one unified model.

The core LGRT architecture, built as a principled adaptation of VGGT for avatar reconstruction (replacing DPT with an MLP GS head, adding FLAME-vertex 3D prompts, and multi-granular camera/expression/pose encodings), is a reasonable and well-motivated design.

Landmark tracking loss and sliced fusion loss are sensible mechanisms for supervising incremental Gaussian aggregation and are shown via ablation (Table 2) to be important for registration quality as frame count grows.

Extensive empirical validation: comparisons at 1/4/8/16 views against four baselines (LAM, MonoGaussianAvatar, GaussianAvatars, and qualitatively Avat3r/GPAvatar), plus additional cross-dataset tests on INSTA, Nersemble, and Ava256, wide-viewpoint generalization (±45°), and streaming/chunked incremental reconstruction — this breadth of experiments is a real strength.

Ablation studies are thorough, covering each architectural/loss component as well as robustness to noisy FLAME landmark tracking, and both quantitative metrics and qualitative visualizations are provided.

The paper is transparent about limitations (LBS/FLAME topology constraints, inability to capture wrinkles, eye gaze, tongue) and includes a reasonably complete reproducibility appendix with hyperparameters and training details.

FastAvatar shows a compelling quality-speed tradeoff curve, improving quality monotonically with more input frames (unlike LAM, which degrades), which directly supports the paper's central incremental-reconstruction claim.
weaknesses: The comparison with Avat3r is not conducted under a fully controlled setting — the paper explicitly states it reuses numbers/qualitative results directly from the Avat3r paper rather than reproducing it locally, which weakens the rigor of this specific comparison despite the stated rationale (no public implementation).

The LAM* baseline was modified by the authors themselves to allow multi-frame fusion; while described as fair, this custom modification of a competitor's method introduces potential bias and is not independently verifiable given code has not yet been released.

Rendering/modeling speed degrades substantially with more input frames (FPS drops from ~240 to ~17.65, modeling time grows from 1.33s to 26.06s from 1 to 16 views), and the number of Gaussian points grows roughly linearly with frame count even after pruning (12.8K→138.9K in the ablation setting) — the practical scalability of the "incremental" paradigm for large numbers of frames is only partially addressed (via FramePack-style compression), and long-sequence scaling behavior is only shown in limited qualitative examples (Fig. 5, 11).

Training relies on 8 H100 GPUs for 14 days on data derived from a single studio dataset (NeRSemble, only 12 constrained camera views), which limits reproducibility for most research groups and raises questions about how well the "unified" model generalizes to truly diverse, uncontrolled "daily capture" conditions (varying lighting, occlusion, non-frontal poses, low-quality phone cameras) beyond the few additional benchmarks tested.

Some methodological details are underspecified, e.g., how camera pose/head pose are estimated at inference time for truly casual/uncalibrated captures, and how sensitive the pipeline is to FLAME tracking failures in more challenging in-the-wild scenarios (the robustness ablation only tests small pixel-level landmark noise, not systematic tracking failure).

Minor presentation issues remain (e.g., typo "MonoGaussianAvata" in Table 1, inconsistent capitalization of "Avatar"), and code/models are not yet available for verification, so independent reproducibility cannot currently be assessed.
